Memoir + family vlogging.

Franke details what her life was like growing up and being exploited on her mother's viral family vlog.

Read if you love...
- memoirs
- family vlogs

To be honest, I went into this one fairly blind after seeing a couple people post about it. I didn't follow their family vlog when it was live, but understand enough of family vlogs to get the point.

Something I found incredibly fascinating throughout this whole book is the way Shari constantly had to walk the fine line of being agreeable to her mother to stay safe, despite knowing even at a young age how the outside world would perceive that. Especially as she got older and left the house for college, in wanting to try to protect herself and her younger siblings.

One of the things I loved is that Shari only named one of her siblings and clarified why she would not be naming her younger siblings (all underage). She has made it a point to keep their private life offline since their mother was arrested, and is actively fighting for laws in Utah to protect minors within the family vlogging world.

So much of this just had me in a constant state of "what the f" and "I can't believe these kids experienced this every single day!"

If you can stomach the content warnings, I highly recommend this!

Representation: PTSD; anxiety; depression; panic attacks

Overview & Thoughts

House of My Mother is a harrowing and deeply personal memoir by Shari Franke, detailing her experiences growing up under the control of her mother, Ruby Franke. Through raw and unfiltered storytelling, Shari sheds light on the emotional, psychological, and physical abuse she endured—experiences that ultimately led to her escape from the toxic environment her mother created.

This book is both heartbreaking and eye-opening, offering an inside look at how manipulation, neglect, and extreme parenting ideologies can devastate a child’s sense of self. Shari’s resilience shines through as she recounts the painful journey of breaking free and reclaiming her life.

Spoilers & Key Themes

🔹 Parental Control & Manipulation – Shari details how Ruby Franke’s authoritarian parenting went beyond discipline, crossing into emotional and physical harm. The book reveals chilling insights into the toxic belief systems that fueled this abuse.

🔹 Breaking Free from Abuse – The memoir follows Shari’s realization that her upbringing was not normal or acceptable, leading to her courageous decision to step away from her mother’s control.

🔹 Survivor’s Perspective – Unlike outside media coverage of the Franke family, this memoir is a firsthand account from someone who lived it. Shari’s voice is powerful in exposing the truth behind the facade her mother presented online.

Memorable Quotes

📌 “If the real world wouldn’t change for me, I had to change for the real world.”
📌 “Nobody just survives something like this and walks away fine.”

Final Thoughts

This memoir is a must-read for those seeking to understand the realities of parental abuse, manipulation, and the long road to healing. It’s not an easy read, but it’s an important one—especially in a world where social media often masks the truth behind seemingly perfect families.

Review Body:
"The House of My Mother" by Shari Franke is a complex and deeply unsettling memoir that pulls back the curtain on a family whose public image masked a disturbing reality. For those familiar with the Franke family blog, this book offers a chillingly intimate look at the events that led to Ruby Franke's conviction for horrific child abuse. Shari, with a fragile strength that belies the trauma she endured, navigates her childhood with a raw honesty that's both captivating and heartbreaking.
Franke doesn't shy away from the difficult truths. She paints a portrait of a mother obsessed with perfection, a pursuit that warped into something deeply toxic and ultimately abusive. The book subtly reveals how Ruby's adherence to certain ideologies, bordering on cult-like devotion, warped her perception of parenting, turning discipline into cruelty. While the book doesn't explicitly focus on the specifics of the Mormon faith, it's impossible to ignore the context of the family's religious background and how certain interpretations may have contributed to Ruby's rigid worldview. Shari's narrative isn't about assigning blame but rather about understanding the insidious nature of control and how easily it can escalate into abuse.
What's particularly striking is Shari's vulnerability. She's not a victim seeking pity, but a young woman trying to make sense of her past. She grapples with the love she still holds for her mother alongside the undeniable pain she experienced. This nuanced portrayal of a complicated relationship is what makes the book so compelling.
"The House of My Mother" also raises crucial questions about the ethics of exposing children online. Shari's story underscores the inherent vulnerability of children whose lives are documented and shared without their consent. It highlights the privacy violations, the potential for bullying and targeting by predators, and the fundamental lack of agency these children have in shaping their own narrative. How can we justify a system that allows parents to turn their children into public figures before they are even old enough to understand the implications? Shari's experience serves as a stark reminder of the potential harm, and it's a conversation we desperately need to be having.
This isn't an easy read, but it's a necessary one. "The House of My Mother" is more than just a memoir; it's a cautionary tale about the dangers of unchecked ideology, the insidious nature of abuse, and the urgent need to protect children, both online and offline. It's a testament to Shari's resilience and a powerful reminder that even in the face of unimaginable trauma, the human spirit can endure.
